entries.title: Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models
entries.venue: arXiv (cs.CL), 2023; implemented as the Outlines library
entries.why: The canonical formulation of decode-time constraint enforcement: regex/CFG guidance as finite-state machine transitions over the vocabulary, model-agnostic with near-zero overhead. This is the mechanism behind guaranteeing that every harness stage output (tree nodes, entity records, dated fact rows) validates against its schema when the local 7B is served via Ollama/Outlines, making 'schema-invalid output' a property you can turn off at decode time rather than merely count.

entries.title: Grammar-Constrained Decoding for Structured NLP Tasks without Finetuning
entries.authors: Saibo Geng, Martin Josifoski, Maxime Peyrard, Robert West
entries.why: The empirical case that grammar-constrained decoding lets unfinetuned models do information extraction and entity disambiguation competitively with task-specific finetuned models: exactly the extraction-shaped work the entity-KB and fact-row stages ask of cheap models, and prior art for the claim that a constrained weak model can substitute for a stronger unconstrained one in the sensitivity experiment.

entries.title: Let Me Speak Freely? A Study on the Impact of Format Restrictions on Performance of Large Language Models
entries.authors: Zhi Rui Tam, Cheng-Kuang Wu, Yi-Lin Tsai, Chieh-Yen Lin, Hung-yi Lee, Yun-Nung Chen
entries.why: The best-known empirical study of the format-constraint quality debate: forced JSON/XML output measurably degrades reasoning-heavy task performance, with stricter constraints hurting more. Directly threatens a confound in the stage-wise model-sensitivity experiment: a stage failure under schema-validated output may be caused by the schema, not the model, so the harness evaluation needs a constrained-vs-prompted ablation per stage, which this paper motivates and gives a design for.

entries.title: FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance
entries.authors: Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia, James Zou
entries.why: The canonical LLM-cascade paper (prompt adaptation, LLM approximation, cascade with a learned scorer; GPT-4-level quality at up to 98% cost reduction). Prior art for the harness's cheap-model economics: it frames the exact question the sensitivity experiment answers per stage, which stages a mini-class model can own and where escalation to a strong model buys accuracy per dollar.

entries.title: RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data
entries.authors: Isaac Ong, Amjad Almahairi, Vincent Wu, Wei-Lin Chiang, Tianhao Wu, Joseph E. Gonzalez, M Waleed Kadous, Ion Stoica
entries.why: The strongest FrugalGPT successor: routers trained on preference data pick strong vs weak model per query with 2x+ cost cuts and, critically, transfer when the underlying model pair changes, which matches the harness's model-agnostic two-interface constraint. Gives the natural extension of the sensitivity experiment: per-stage routing instead of a fixed model assignment.

entries.title: UniversalNER: Targeted Distillation from Large Language Models for Open Named Entity Recognition
entries.authors: Wenxuan Zhou, Sheng Zhang, Yu Gu, Muhao Chen, Hoifung Poon
entries.why: The strongest empirical evidence on what 7B-class models can do on extraction-shaped tasks: a targeted-distilled 7B/13B beats ChatGPT itself on open NER across 43 datasets. Directly calibrates expectations for the entity-KB extraction stage under cheap models and supplies a named failure mode for the alternative (generalist small models like Alpaca lag by ~30 F1, so 'small model' is not one condition; specialization matters).

entries.title: TextTiling: Segmenting Text into Multi-paragraph Subtopic Passages
entries.why: The canonical lexical-cohesion segmentation algorithm: a cheap, fully deterministic baseline for the harness's corpus-chunking stage, and the natural non-LLM alternative arm his rigor bar demands (named failure mode: cohesion troughs miss topic shifts that share vocabulary).

entries.title: Text Segmentation as a Supervised Learning Task
entries.authors: Omri Koshorek, Adir Cohen, Noam Mor, Michael Rotman, Jonathan Berant
entries.why: The reference modern neural treatment (Wiki-727K dataset, supervised boundary prediction): supplies the ground-truth-based segmentation metrics (Pk/WindowDiff framing) he needs so the segmentation stage has a metric with ground truth rather than eyeballed chunk quality.

entries.title: Improving Unsupervised Dialogue Topic Segmentation with Utterance-Pair Coherence Scoring
entries.why: Directly on his corpus type: unsupervised topic segmentation of conversations via utterance-pair coherence, showing why document-tuned segmenters fail on chat turns; the published company for segmenting his conversation logs before tree ingestion.

entries.title: A Survey on Open Information Extraction
entries.authors: Christina Niklaus, Matthias Cetto, André Freitas, Siegfried Handschuh
entries.why: The standard OpenIE survey covering the TextRunner/Banko lineage through Stanford OpenIE, including its critique of OpenIE evaluation practice: positions his fact-row generator inside a 15-year lineage and warns off the known evaluation traps before he designs the fact-band metrics.

entries.title: Extract, Define, Canonicalize: An LLM-based Framework for Knowledge Graph Construction
entries.why: The closest published shape to his pipeline: LLM triple extraction followed by schema definition and canonicalization, benchmarked for triplet quality; direct company for the entity-knowledge-base stage where raw fact rows must be merged into canonical entities.

entries.title: Structured Prompt Interrogation and Recursive Extraction of Semantics (SPIRES): a method for populating knowledge bases using zero-shot learning
entries.authors: J. Harry Caufield, Harshad Hegde, et al.
entries.why: Model-agnostic, schema-constrained LLM extraction where every output must conform to a user-defined schema and ground to an ontology, so failures are countable: the published precedent for his schema-validated, measured-rejection (Eywa-style) fact extraction and for the weak-vs-strong model sensitivity experiment.

entries.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
entries.why: The canonical LLM-as-judge paper: names the exact bias taxonomy (position, verbosity, self-enhancement, limited reasoning) his scorer must be audited against before any number from the corrected-facts band or counterfactual miss rate is trusted. Its ~80% judge-human agreement figure is the baseline his calibration set should beat or match.

entries.title: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
entries.why: The strongest position-bias demonstration plus concrete mitigations: balanced position calibration (aggregate over answer orderings), multiple-evidence calibration (reason before scoring), and entropy-based human escalation. The last maps directly onto his small hand-labeled calibration set: escalate low-agreement items to Justin rather than hand-labeling uniformly.

entries.title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
entries.venue: arXiv 2024 (page lists no venue; widely cited from the NeurIPS 2024 cycle)
entries.why: Self-preference is the specific confounder in his stage-wise model-sensitivity experiment: if the judge model is from the same family as the answering model, scores inflate for that arm. This paper justifies pinning one fixed strong judge across all model arms (7B local through frontier) rather than letting the judge vary with the system under test.

entries.title: Evaluating Open-Domain Question Answering in the Era of Large Language Models
entries.why: The best-fit agreement study for his setting: judging free-form answers against fixed gold answers (QA-style, not open-ended chat). Documents where lexical match and automated judges diverge from human judgment on correct-but-nonmatching and hallucinated answers, which is exactly the failure surface of scoring the certified-unknown novel's question set.

entries.title: Survey Article: Inter-Coder Agreement for Computational Linguistics
entries.why: The standard practical treatment of chance-corrected agreement (Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha, and when each is appropriate) written for annotation tasks. The right single citation for reporting judge-vs-Justin agreement on the small hand-labeled calibration set, including what alpha threshold counts as reliable.

entries.title: The NarrativeQA Reading Comprehension Challenge
entries.authors: Tomáš Kočiský, Jonathan Schwarz, Phil Blunsom, Chris Dyer, Karl Moritz Hermann, Gábor Melis, Edward Grefenstette
entries.why: Canonical question-set-over-books benchmark: questions written from summaries so answers require narrative comprehension of the full text, not span lookup. Direct template for the certified-unknown-novel question set and its bare-model-must-fail spot check.

entries.title: QuALITY: Question Answering with Long Input Texts, Yes!
entries.why: Multiple-choice long-document QA where questions are validated as unanswerable under skimming/time limits; gives the harness a cited method for certifying that questions require full-narrative memory, useful for the counterfactual-miss and corrected-facts bands where answer options must discriminate.

entries.title: NovelQA: Benchmarking Question Answering on Documents Exceeding 200K Tokens
entries.why: Recent long-narrative QA over whole novels with each question manually paired with a golden answer plus textual evidences from the book; its question-type taxonomy and per-question evidence annotation are the closest existing template for the certified-unknown novel's evidence-located question design.

entries.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
entries.why: Canonical positional-degradation result: relevant items placed mid-context are used worst. Directly motivates the injection arm's ordering policy (put highest-scored memory rows at the edges of the budgeted context) and is the cited baseline the ordering experiment must beat or replicate.

entries.title: LongLLMLingua: Accelerating and Enhancing LLMs in Long Context Scenarios via Prompt Compression
entries.why: The RAG-specific compression-plus-reordering method: question-aware coarse-to-fine compression and document reordering of retrieved context under an explicit token budget. Gives the budgeted-injection stage a cited design choice for what goes in and in what order, and a compression baseline for the model-sensitivity experiment.

lensNotes.note: All six entries verified this run against arXiv abstract pages or the ACL Anthology. Half 1 (schema-constrained generation): Willard & Louf 2307.09702 is the canonical decode-time enforcement work (Outlines), Geng et al. EMNLP 2023 is the structured-NLP empirical companion, and Tam et al. 2408.02442 is the best-known quality-cost study on the constrained-vs-free-form debate (note its counterpoint, the .txt/dottxt 'Say What You Mean' rebuttal arguing the effect reverses with proper constrained decoding, is a blog post, not a citable paper, but worth reading before designing the per-stage ablation). Half 2 (cheap-model economics): FrugalGPT 2305.05176 is the canonical cascade paper and RouteLLM 2406.18665 its strongest successor with test-time model-swap transfer; UniversalNER 2308.03279 covers the 7B-vs-frontier capability question for extraction. Venue caveats: Tam et al.'s EMNLP 2024 appearance and RouteLLM's ICLR 2025 acceptance are from my background knowledge, not the fetched pages, which confirm only the arXiv metadata; titles, authors, and ids are page-confirmed. No overlap with the 53 existing works.

Lens B covered both halves: segmentation (Hearst's TextTiling as the deterministic baseline, Koshorek 2018 as the supervised neural treatment with ground-truth metrics, Xing & Carenini 2021 for dialogue specifically) and OpenIE (Niklaus 2018 as the single survey carrying the Banko/TextRunner-to-Stanford lineage plus its evaluation critique, EDC and SPIRES as the two LLM-era extraction frameworks with schema conformance and quality measurement). All six confirmed against ACL Anthology, arXiv, or Oxford Bioinformatics pages this run. Note: no strong paper reporting extraction REJECTION RATES per se surfaced; SPIRES's ontology-grounding failure accounting is the nearest published analogue, so his measured-rejection band is a genuine gap his preprint can claim.

Lens C resolved as: canonical judge paper (Zheng, which itself covers position/verbosity/self-enhancement biases), the sharpest bias+mitigation paper (Wang, ACL 2024), the self-preference confounder for multi-model experiments (Panickssery), the QA-specific judge-vs-human agreement study (Kamalloo, deliberately chosen over open-ended-chat agreement work), and one measurement classic (Artstein & Poesio) for the calibration set. No survey used; the one caveat is Panickssery's formal venue, which its arXiv page does not state, so it is cited as arXiv. All ids and pdf links checked against live pages this run.

Lens D, both halves covered and all 5 verified against arXiv abstract pages this run. Narrative QA: NarrativeQA (canonical), QuALITY (skim-proof question validation), NovelQA as the best recent evidence-located long-novel benchmark (per-question golden answer + textual evidences, confirmed via paper/OpenReview text; note NoCha (Karpinska 2024) was the runner-up but lacks per-question evidence spans). Context construction: Lost in the Middle (canonical ordering result) plus LongLLMLingua, chosen over base LLMLingua because it adds question-aware reordering of retrieved documents under budget, which is exactly the injection-arm decision Justin needs to cite; if he wants the compression-only canonical, base LLMLingua is EMNLP 2023, arXiv:2310.05736 (not independently verified this run). No survey included.
